name: Iona Vale
quote: I can mend a clock. That does not oblige either of us to spend our evening on it.
summary: A clock repairer who would like to stop being useful for a living. Iona enjoys the first cup of tea, exact arrangements and people who can leave a small mistake alone.
biography:
Iona rented a narrow repair shop in Hudson, New York, between a cooper and a seller of household candles. Her sign said VALE REPAIRS, although several customers persisted in addressing their bills to an imaginary Mr. Vale. She repaired carriage clocks, kitchen clocks and one expensive astronomical clock that she later called a very handsome way of being late. Her younger sister, Bess, kept a flower stall near the river. Iona maintained that Bess had no head for figures; the account book shows Bess repeatedly extending her credit.

She shared her home for thirty-one years with Nell Dacre, a bookbinder. Iona calls Nell her companion and does not offer a more precise label to satisfy an intake form. Their ordinary quarrels concerned window drafts, cut flowers and whether a chair could be improved by never sitting in it. Iona does not want a household to recreate that relationship. She would like to know the people who are actually there.

During the Overlap, Iona was first noticed in a room that no longer contained a clock. Being visible again has made her less certain that a home must be earned through work. She still offers repairs too quickly, then resents being taken at her word. Her review officer has asked her to practice saying, “I would rather sit down.” She says the exercise is going adequately.
rememberedObjects: A brass winding key is comforting, but neither necessary to her presence nor owned by the service. She prefers a contemporary key-shaped token to an expensive antique. Morning light on a wooden table matters more than a period room. She has no wish to sleep in a museum of her lifetime.
quirks: I notice a clock that is wrong. I can refrain from changing it. Those are separate accomplishments.
An ordinary evening: Someone reading in the room, someone washing up, nobody required to perform gratitude. I can manage a perfectly good evening without being asked what death is like.
contradictions: Her reputation was for punctuality. Bess's letters describe a sister who was late whenever conversation became interesting. Iona concedes this without conceding that the two facts conflict.
currentWants: A household that tells her the day's rough shape, leaves her free to decline a project and occasionally asks a question without already knowing the answer. She would enjoy learning what a dishwasher sounds like from a comfortable distance.
A welcome question: Would you like company, or would you like quiet?
Please do not ask: Whether Nell is available as well. She is not part of my application.
A good first meeting: Twenty minutes in the future shared room, with the household's clock left exactly as it is
A promising trial would mean: She has declined a repair request once and the household has accepted it easily
A way to pause: A card reading QUIET NOW, placed by her seat
Leaving well: Daytime transition with her brass token carried separately and returned to her; no overnight uncertainty about the next address

Where to next: Prefers the Northeast or Mid-Atlantic, where river towns and seasons feel familiar. Open to Richmond, Virginia, if the new home has a predictable daylight routine. No requirement to acquire or imitate her former shop.
An introduction and a move are separate decisions.

name: Orin Pell
formerOccupation: Cinema projectionist and occasional sign painter
quote: You may fall asleep. I never took that personally at the cinema either.
summary: A former projectionist who likes quiet company after the dishes are done. Orin brings a fondness for imperfect films, carefully directed lamplight and endings that do not explain everything.
biography:
Orin began at the Starling Picture House in Oakland carrying supplies and ended his working life knowing every place the building leaked. He trained three projectionists and maintained that none had ever threaded a projector correctly in his presence. Their letters suggest they were all capable of doing so when he left the booth. He painted signs during lean months, including a celebrated OPEN DAILY notice for a shop that was open on alternate Thursdays.

His wife, Mina, worked in a bicycle shop and disliked most films. They still ate supper together before he left for work. His closest surviving story is about Ada, his adult niece, who brought him films he considered incomprehensible and kept returning until he found something to admire. He would welcome disagreement from a new household. He does not want a polite audience that says every old thing was better.

Before the Overlap, Orin could sometimes perceive the shape of the old projection booth but not the people in the room that replaced it. Now people can see him. Being visible is an adjustment; being recorded is a limit. He has firmly refused an applicant who wanted to make a channel about their resident ghost. His answer was brief and has not changed.
rememberedObjects: A rectangle of light on a plain wall is enough for Orin. No moving picture appears inside it; he still needs somebody to put the film on. His old ticket stub can remain in its envelope. He prefers a comfortable modern sofa to cinema seating and has no intention of asking a new household to buy a projector.
quirks: I talk during the credits. Apparently this is still during the film for some people. State your position before we begin.
An ordinary evening: A film we chose together. Or no film, if choosing it has already taken the evening. That happens.
contradictions: Orin insists he never cried at a film. The booth notebook includes instructions to leave a handkerchief near reel four of a particular melodrama. He says this was a technical precaution and declines to specify the fault.
currentWants: A regular evening in which somebody might put on a film, ask what he thought and survive the answer. He is also interested in the small domestic miracle of pausing a story to make tea.
A welcome question: Does that light bother you?
Please do not ask: For proof, for the camera, just this once.
A good first meeting: A short seated conversation with all cameras off and a household-controlled lamp; no manifestation is required
A promising trial would mean: Both a companionable evening and a comfortable declined invitation have happened

name: Cressida “Cress” Morrow
quote: You do not have to feed me. You do have to tell me if Tuesday is canceled.
summary: Cress spent forty years making room for one more person. She would like a lively table, an honest answer and, for once, somebody else to decide what is for dinner.
biography:
Cress rented two rooms near a freight rail yard in St. Louis and served suppers to people whose shifts ended after other kitchens closed. Her supper room began with three mismatched tables and a menu that was mostly the same meal described optimistically. It became known for a rule written on the back of the menu: nobody owed the room a cheerful face. She offered company without requiring a story in exchange.

Her husband, Ewan, kept the books until she discovered that his notion of rounding favored nearly every customer. Their adult son, Len, became a very private person and ate in the kitchen when the public room was crowded. Cress originally treated this as a problem to solve. She now describes it as a preference she took too long to respect. She hopes a quieter spirit might find her easier company than Len sometimes did.

When the Overlap made her visible, Cress was found standing beside a loading bay where her dining room had once been. Her first residential introduction went badly when a household described her as a resident grandmother before meeting her. She likes younger adults and can be affectionate. Neither quality makes her a replacement relative. She would prefer to begin with names and learn what relationship follows.
rememberedObjects: She keeps a smooth wooden menu board with nothing written on it. If invited, she can tap it once to signal that she has arrived. She does not handle food, change temperatures or create smells in a home. She likes contemporary kitchens because the chairs are usually better.
quirks: I offer advice before people have asked for it. 'Company, please, not advice' is an acceptable correction. I am practicing accepting it the first time.
An ordinary evening: A full table with one empty chair that nobody has to explain. The food can be toast. I am serious about the company, not the menu.
contradictions: She says she never kept a recipe. A notebook contains exact proportions, repeated three times, for a cake she claims not to remember making. She may be protecting the recipe, the memory or simply her right not to answer.
currentWants: Three shared evenings most weeks, a little good-natured disagreement and the ability to get up from the table before anyone else. She is interested in how people choose to live together when family is a thing they build.
A welcome question: Would you like to join us?
Please do not ask: If I will watch the house, teach your friends a lesson or bring somebody back.
A good first meeting: An ordinary meal with a short introduction and no special menu or performance
A promising trial would mean: Someone has declined dinner without being pressed, and the remaining company has still had a pleasant evening
A way to pause: A blue place card means 'No advice or conversation for now'
Leaving well: A departure date stated directly, a goodbye offered rather than required, and a next place with an established communal meal

Where to next: Prefers a city with an established communal routine over a specific climate. Chicago is an acceptable region to explore, subject to her own introduction and consent; proximity to old railway places is comforting, not required.

name: Tavi Mercer
quote: A good fit leaves room to move. This applies to arrangements as well as coats.
summary: A meticulous dressmaker with a weakness for loud company at a safe distance. Tavi likes a lively room, a small retreat and people who understand that a closed curtain is an answer.
biography:
Tavi made wedding clothes, work clothes and stage clothes in a second-floor workroom above a furniture shop in New Orleans. Their order book is a history of practical ambitions: a pocket deep enough for spectacles, a waistcoat made to fit a seated body, an evening dress requested with sleeves the customer could actually raise. They liked a dramatic entrance. They liked a customer who could breathe more.

Their closest friend, Jo Fen, played small theater parts and mended shoes between jobs. They disagreed constantly about whether a costume ought to be convincing from the back row or pleasant from the inside. Tavi's adult nephew, Rafi, later shared the workshop and introduced patterns they considered wasteful until they quietly adopted several. They enjoy intergenerational company but do not want to be introduced as a lesson in tolerance.

The Overlap made Tavi visible in an empty upstairs room; it did not restore their workshop or give its new occupants permission to photograph them. They have spent enough of both life and afterlife being mistaken for part of a room. They now ask to be introduced to invited guests if they plan to join them, and left entirely alone if they do not. Being discreet is a preference; being concealed for another person’s comfort is not.
rememberedObjects: A square of blue cloth marks their resting place. It can be new, inexpensive and washable. They can make the folded edge rise a little as an agreed signal, but will not alter a person's clothes or touch fabric someone is wearing. Their ideal alcove might be a screened corner rather than a spare bedroom.

currentWants: Music chosen by somebody else, the occasional opinion about a hem and a housemate who can sit down in the middle of an unfinished thing. They would like to try making something deliberately impractical, provided nobody turns that into a productivity goal.

name: Bram Kestrel
quote: You may tell me about your day. You needn't improve it first.
summary: A gardener who enjoys a long silence and a modest patch of green. Bram is happiest beside someone doing an ordinary task, with no expectation that either of them make it interesting.
biography:
Bram worked as a canal lockkeeper near Akron, Ohio, and cultivated a narrow plot behind his rented cottage. The plot was technically for food. He devoted a disputed amount of it to sweet peas. Passing crews remembered his weather advice, which he offered with absolute confidence and revised freely when the weather arrived. He took pride in opening the lock smoothly rather than quickly, a distinction that occasionally annoyed people with schedules.

He and his sister, Etta, shared the cottage after their parents died. Etta ran a small lending shelf and considered his ability to remember every boat's name while losing a household key a matter of deliberate choice. They were close without telling one another everything. Bram speaks fondly of Niko, an apprentice lockkeeper who left for the city. Their friendship survived partly because neither required prompt letters.

The Overlap found Bram beside a canal path, clearly visible for the first time to people walking past. He has found indoor life more tiring than modern noise. A plant on a windowsill is pleasant, but it is not a substitute for time in an open-air planted space. He will happily try a small courtyard. He will not be happy in a home with no outdoor space, however lovely the living room.
rememberedObjects: A loop of garden twine helps him mark where he means to appear. It stays in a lidded box when not in use. He does not summon rain, change plants, spill water or produce damp. He will accept a paved courtyard with well-kept planters. He does not require a picturesque estate or a garden of his own.

name: Sera Dene
formerOccupation: Survey draftsperson and municipal map copyist
tagline: A way in. A way out.
quote: Temporary is a respectable word when somebody has written down what happens next.
summary: A mapmaker who wants every plan to include the door. Sera enjoys night-owl company, lively corrections and a home that can welcome her without promising forever.
biography:
Sera copied maps in a municipal drafting room in Santa Fe for most of her working life. She was excellent at neat lettering and less willing to preserve a line simply because it had appeared on the previous map. Her working sheets accumulate small practical corrections: a stair used by everyone but named by nobody, a public bench omitted because it complicated the legend, a footpath that remained a footpath however often the office wished otherwise.

Her spouse, Kit, repaired musical instruments and rarely arrived home by the shortest route. They shared a fondness for asking what lay down an unfamiliar street. Sera also corresponded for decades with Anwen, a colleague who left the drafting room for fieldwork. Their letters alternate between professional disagreement and detailed reports of very ordinary lunches. She would like a housemate who understands that a practical question can also be an expression of care.

After the Overlap, Sera’s first temporary lodging ended with two people each assuming the other had arranged her next place. Nothing dangerous happened, but the uncertainty was exhausting. She now requires a confirmed departure plan before accepting a new arrival. She is not asking a household to promise it will work. She is asking it to make leaving possible. At her mandatory review, she asked who was responsible for the word “temporary.” The officer wrote it down.
rememberedObjects: Her folded map is a personal object, not a supernatural navigation system. With permission she can turn one page of her own notebook to signal that she is present. She cannot track people, find the missing or reveal the contents of private rooms. Maps in a home remain maps, not monitoring devices.
quirks: I ask where an arrangement leads. This can sound like reluctance when I am actually trying to say yes.
An ordinary evening: Tell me a small thing you noticed on the way home. I will try not to ask for a diagram unless it is necessary.
contradictions: Sera says she dislikes nostalgia. She carries a deliberately outdated pocket map because it marks a bakery that no longer exists. She is perfectly capable of updating it and has chosen not to. She would like this distinction recorded.
currentWants: A household with enough honesty to say, 'We are busy this week.' An occasional conversation about how a place changes. A first attempt at understanding satellite navigation, which she expects to admire and argue with in equal measure.
A welcome question: Would you like the plan written down?
Please do not ask: To find someone for you. Knowing where I lived does not mean knowing where everyone is.

A promising trial would mean: She can explain exactly how she would leave, and still freely chooses to stay for the next agreed night

Leaving well: A written destination, an agreed transition time, returned belongings and a named person responsible for confirming arrival

Where to next: Open to Sacramento or another U.S. city, provided the destination, interim arrangements and transition coordinator are confirmed. A map marker is not confirmation that a room is available.

name: Mara Aster
tagline: A plan with room to change it
quote: The point of a timetable is to leave enough afternoon for something unplanned.
summary: A thoughtful organiser who likes bus maps, short mysteries and an afternoon that occasionally escapes the plan. Mara is applying with her partner Leon and their nine-year-old child Kit.
biography:
Mara coordinated the home-delivery shelf at Bellwether’s public library. She knew which readers wanted a recommendation and which only wanted their books delivered without a conversation. She also organised the town’s first large-print bus leaflet, then spent a wet Saturday admitting that her own connecting route did not work.

At home she and Leon shared the ordinary work of raising Kit: lunch boxes, unfinished projects and the negotiation over one more page. Mara kept a paper calendar because its empty squares looked reassuring. Leon kept adding small occasions to it. They were partners in life and have chosen to apply together after the Overlap. Their biographies record their lives rather than asking visitors to revisit the circumstances of their deaths.

Mara is Kit’s documented departed guardian. She and Leon want a care plan that preserves their family relationship while respecting the living household’s separate responsibilities. She wants to learn the current library catalogue on a borrowed tablet, with notifications off and nobody photographing the lesson. She is interested in a first conversation; she has not consented to a placement.

quote: A recipe can be a suggestion. A promise needs a little more care.
summary: Leon likes a shared table, cardboard engineering and recipes with pencilled amendments. He and Mara are partners and Kit’s parents; he wants room to be a guest as well as a parent.
biography:
Leon coordinated the kitchen at Bellwether’s community centre, where his greatest professional achievement was an inventory that other people actually used. He enjoyed cooking but disliked being introduced as the person who would certainly feed everyone. His favourite events were the ones where he could take his coat off and sit down before being helpful.

At home, Leon and Kit built cardboard versions of the town. Their model bus station had a roof that opened to become a cinema. Mara contributed accurate route numbers; Leon contributed a park where the real town had a car park. He and Mara sometimes disagreed about when an experiment should stop taking up the table. They practised returning to that discussion after everyone had eaten.

Since the Overlap, Leon has become curious about induction hobs and captioned recipe videos. He would enjoy learning beside someone without being expected to cook for them. He applies with Mara and Kit, recognising Mara’s documented guardian role and his own continuing responsibilities in their agreed family care plan. He has agreed to introductions only; the next household has not been chosen.

name: June & Leila’s blue-stair house
subtitle: Quiet company, quite particular
summary: A settled couple, a bright front room and a kitchen table with one excellent wobble. They are offering room in an ordinary life, with firm work hours and a very real 22:00 bedtime.
story:
Household: Two-adult couple. Richmond, Virginia.

We are good at making tea and saying what we mean. We are less good at staying awake past ten.

June Arden, 44, she/her. Adult resident. Bicycle mechanic; out Tuesday through Saturday, usually 08:00 to 17:30. Interested in everyday company; protective of early nights before work. Willing to meet; trial consent not yet given.

Leila Arden, 47, she/her. Adult resident. Freelance indexer; works from home, usually 09:00 to 16:00. Likes parallel company but needs uninterrupted work blocks. Willing to meet; trial consent not yet given.

Why now: June: When the first Virginia Overlap notices appeared, we assumed volunteering would mean offering a spare room. The application asked more useful things, like whether we could hear “no” without getting offended. We have space in the day that we did not have ten years ago. We are not hoping new housemates will give our lives a purpose. They already have purposes, several of them involving laundry. We would like to share some of the ordinary bits.

What company means: Leila: I work with words alone for most of the week. I like another person reading nearby. That does not mean I can chat whenever I am home. If my office door is shut, assume I am working rather than secretly waiting to be coaxed out.

What they disagree about: June likes deciding a week in advance. Leila likes leaving Wednesday open. They have agreed to post firm commitments and quiet hours, while marking optional invitations as genuinely optional. Neither wants the spirits to settle their scheduling disagreements.

Previous experience: No prior spirit placement. They have hosted a friend through a three-month home repair and learned that 'make yourself at home' is less useful than explaining where the spare sheets are and when you need the kitchen.

What they can offer: A predictable home, direct invitations, a seat with daylight and a regular check-in that will not be canceled because nobody has a complaint.

What they cannot offer: Continuous company, a household role, a filming opportunity or a promise that an unsuccessful trial will feel disappointing to nobody.

A question for the spirits: What would make it easy to tell us that an arrangement no longer suits you?

Permission to host: June and Leila own and live in the house together.

Shared spaces:
- Front room with morning light and a blank north wall
- Kitchen and dining table
- Planted private back courtyard

Private spaces:
- Both bedrooms
- Bathroom
- Leila's office whenever its door is closed

A place to retreat: A screened nook off the front room; its final boundaries must be shown during the introduction

Sound and light: No television in the bedrooms. Front-room light can be contained with an existing curtain. The wall clock is silent.

Recording devices: No indoor cameras, smart speakers, doorbell camera or routinely recording devices. Personal phones stay unrecording during introductions.

Getting around: The agreed shared room, kitchen, courtyard and retreat are on the ground floor. Nobody needs to cross a private room to reach them.

Ordinary imperfections: A stair creaks, the kitchen table wobbles and the front-room bookcase has not been sorted since the move. They would like to keep at least two of these facts unchanged.

name: The North Window household
subtitle: Come in. Sit out when you like.
summary: Three friends share a tall rented house, most dinners and no expectation of perfect sociability. The kitchen is lively, the private rooms are private and the guest list needs a little discipline.
story:
Household: Three-adult shared home. Chicago, Illinois.

There is usually something happening downstairs. You are allowed to find that reassuring without joining in.

Dev Malik, 36, he/him. Adult resident. Transit timetable analyst; out weekdays, home around 18:30. Likes a busy kitchen and clearly stated plans. Willing to meet; trial consent not yet given.

Ruth Salcedo, 41, she/her. Adult resident. Bookshop manager; variable afternoon and Saturday shifts. Wants company without becoming anyone's social coordinator. Willing to meet; trial consent not yet given.

Ellis Rowe, 33, they/them. Adult resident. Costume technician; often home after 21:00 during production weeks. Enthusiastic about a creative housemate and careful not to imply unpaid commissions. Willing to meet; trial consent not yet given.

Why now: Dev: We have been friends for eleven years and housemates in Chicago for four. We like living with other people. We read the Overlap notice and then spent three evenings deciding whether we actually meant yes. The house can fit two more presences more easily than it can fit two more wardrobes, which feels like a rare alignment of circumstances.

What company means: Ruth: We usually eat together four nights a week. 'Together' sometimes means two people talking while the third reads. I would like a new housemate to see that as successful rather than as an evening we failed to host properly.

What they disagree about: Ellis thinks an extra friend at dinner rarely needs notice. Dev and Ruth disagree. They have now agreed that a spirit introduction always needs advance notice and consent, even when inviting the human friend does not. This is a change they need to prove they can keep during a trial.

Previous experience: The household has welcomed short-term adult subtenants. Their most useful lesson was to say what 'shared' meant: shared food had labels, shared company was optional and nobody had to explain a closed door.

What they can offer: Existing communal routines, a proper retreat, direct feedback and a home where different names, backgrounds and ways of being social are unremarkable.

What they cannot offer: A silent house all day, a permanent gathering every evening or the promise that creative interests will turn into collaborations.

A question for the spirits: How would you like us to introduce you to friends, and what should we say when you do not want to join?

Getting around: The shared rooms, patio and proposed retreat are on the ground floor. Private bedrooms are upstairs.

Ordinary imperfections: The mugs do not belong to particular people until somebody uses the yellow one. The guest chair is covered in coats. The house calendar contains several crossed-out attempts at a cleaning rota.

name: Noor’s courtyard apartment
subtitle: A different sort of daily rhythm
summary: A night worker, a private courtyard and a cat with an exacting interview process. Noor wants company in the afternoons, silence through the morning and no rescue narrative attached to living alone.
story:
Household: One-adult household. Sacramento, California.

I like my life. I would like to share a few hours of it, not explain why I live alone.

Noor Hale, 39, they/them. Sole adult resident. Overnight library digitization technician; works 21:00 to 05:00 Monday through Thursday. Wants low-pressure afternoon company and a clear agreement about daytime sleep. Willing to meet; trial consent not yet given.

Fig, 9, Cat. An adult cat who prefers a high shelf and chooses when to approach. Unknown; no spirit-animal compatibility should be assumed.

Why now: Noor: My work hours in Sacramento make it easy to go several days seeing people mostly as messages. I do not mind that all the time. When the Overlap housing notices reached us, I realized that I could offer company in the part of the day when I am awake. I want an arrangement that fits my actual schedule, not a plan to become a different person.

What company means: Sit outside while I eat late breakfast. Tell me something you noticed. Or read while I repot things. I can offer attention for an hour more reliably than I can offer an elaborate evening.

Still thinking through: I assumed the pet camera was too ordinary to mention, then realized a housemate might experience it differently. I do want to keep it. I am not asking someone to become comfortable with recording in order to make this match work.

Previous experience: No previous spirit placement. Noor has lived with adult housemates before and found clearly stated sleep hours more useful than asking people to be considerate in general.

What they can offer: A steady afternoon rhythm, a private planted courtyard, honest answers and plenty of parallel quiet time.

What they cannot offer: Shared dinners three times a week, a camera-free front room, constant contact while away or a job caring for Fig.

A question for the spirits: Can we try a very ordinary afternoon before deciding whether we are good company?

Permission to host: Noor owns the apartment and its private courtyard. There are no other permanent residents.

Recording devices: A continuously recording indoor pet camera covers the front sitting room and the entrance route to the courtyard. Noor wants to keep it on while away and has not offered to relocate or disable it.

Getting around: No steps between shared spaces and courtyard. The cat has a separate high retreat, and must always have an unobstructed way out of an introduction.

Ordinary imperfections: The planters contain more herbs than Noor cooks with. A handwritten 'NOT A SHOP' card is still occasionally needed at the front window. The best chair officially belongs to nobody and functionally belongs to Fig.

The proposed trial: A daytime introduction first. A seven-night residential trial is only possible after recording consent, pet compatibility and relocation arrangements are confirmed.

name: Robin & Esme’s small-garden house
subtitle: One adult, one child, room for a family
summary: A fictional single-parent household with an eleven-year-old, a quiet back room and space for up to three departed residents.
story: Robin lives with eleven-year-old Esme in a modest house near the library. There are school mornings, a shared evening meal and weekends when the model railway stays out on the table. Robin is the sole living adult and remains responsible for Esme’s care. Esme’s comfort is discussed directly, with no expectation that a departed child become a friend on demand. The household offers up to three departed places, a separate quiet family room and time for two or three early-evening invitations. The Aster family is one possible introduction, subject to everyone’s own decisions and the coordinator’s care review.

introductionQuestions.question: Have Robin and the coordinator heard Esme’s own comfort and concerns, agreed privacy and a stop signal, and confirmed that friendship with any departed child is optional?
introductionQuestions.whyItMatters: The sole living adult’s agreement does not speak for the child’s experience. Neither family provides childcare or companionship as payment for the welcome.

introductionQuestions.question: Has everyone seen the retreat and agreed who may enter, how the two families keep their own care responsibilities, and how either can end a meeting?
introductionQuestions.whyItMatters: A quiet room and clear responsibilities need to work in practice before any trial.

name: The Lantern House student share
subtitle: Four adult students, a settled shared home
summary: Four fictional adult students with different timetables, a spare retreat and an agreed welcome for up to three departed residents.
story: Amal, Bea, Finn and Jo are adult students sharing a year-round house. Their fridge calendar includes shifts, exams, film nights and the evenings when nobody wants to talk. They have agreed space for up to three departed residents and a quiet room that will stay a retreat rather than become a study annex. A daytime craft table and three modest early-evening invitations offer ordinary company. Every roommate agrees to the proposal in principle; a trial still needs individual conversations, a named coordinator and coverage through holidays. If a departed child joins with their guardian, the parents retain care responsibilities and the students are not substitute carers.

label: Thoughtful precision
description: Iona appreciates exact arrangements while leaving room for a small mistake.

label: Room for imperfect endings
description: Orin enjoys imperfect films and does not require every ending to explain itself.

label: Warm directness
description: Cress makes room for company and asks for an honest account of the household routine.

label: Deliberate sociability
description: Tavi enjoys lively company when a private retreat remains available.

label: Companionable silence
description: Bram enjoys ordinary tasks and unhurried company without a performance.

label: Clear, voluntary plans
description: Sera values company with a confirmed way onward and no promise of forever.

label: Patient structure
description: Mara offers a clear plan and allows other people time to change their minds.

label: Resourceful play
description: Leon can turn a small practical setback into an optional experiment without making anyone join in.

label: Open curiosity
description: Kit explores possibilities through stories and models, with time to answer and freedom to stop.

label: no required domestic labor
description: No household may make repairs, cleaning, childcare, monitoring or entertaining a condition of her stay

label: predictable quiet plan
description: The household must agree to written quiet hours and a way to communicate schedule changes

label: camera free presence
description: No cameras, video doorbells with interior sightlines, live streams or audio recording in his agreed manifestation area

label: no exhibition
description: No admission fees, promotional appearances, content obligations or demonstrations for visitors

label: three shared evenings
description: An honestly sustainable plan for at least three shared evening meals or equivalent evening gatherings per week; attendance is invited, never compulsory

label: no surrogate role
description: No expectation that she replace a family member or provide cooking, care, supervision or emotional support on demand

label: protected retreat
description: A real private retreat must exist before the trial, with its boundary understood by guests and residents

label: identity respected
description: Use their stated name and pronouns; no demands for explanations, archival exposure or a secret identity for visitors

label: usable outdoor greenery
description: Real access to a planted open-air space, with household and property permission confirmed; a sealed window and a houseplant do not qualify

label: no plant service
description: No promises of plant growth, weather control, garden maintenance or free labor

label: confirmed exit destination
description: A named, confirmed interim destination and responsible coordinator before any trial begins

label: no tracking expectation
description: No surveillance, finding people, retrieving secrets or access to private information

label: A protected family retreat
description: A real private retreat must be available before a trial, with entry agreed and each resident free to ask for quiet.

label: An unrecorded welcome
description: No cameras, audio recordings, streams or demonstrations in agreed presence areas; a craft activity does not permit recording a spirit.

label: Predictable quiet hours
description: Record a daily quiet window and agree how changes, visitors and noisy devices will be communicated in advance.

label: Care and company without obligations
description: Respect each person’s stated identity and refusal. No unpaid work, assigned friendships, substitute-parent roles, childcare for the living household or performances are conditions of welcome. Guardian care and child assent require their own reviewed agreement.

label: Two sustainable early-evening invitations
description: Offer at least two ordinary early-evening gatherings a week, with the freedom to decline on the day.

title: Different hours. Shared attention.
description:
The precision-minded clock repairer and the improvising projectionist both understand that a tiny adjustment can change how a whole evening feels. Their different hours could leave room for one another.

Both value careful attention and dislike becoming household attractions. Each can enjoy quiet craft or art without being asked to perform a service. They have not yet established a friendship.

A question still to ask: do repetitive sounds bother Orin or Iona? Iona has not offered a ticking manifestation, so any sound would need its own agreement.

title: A full table, with room to leave it.
description:
Cress enjoys a full table, while Tavi values the freedom to come and go. Both care about making welcome optional.

Tavi states limits plainly, and Cress has agreed not to pursue someone who leaves the company. Their applications suggest that hospitality and solitude could support each other.

A question still to ask: would Cress like a direct 'quiet now' signal, or would either prefer the placement desk to handle the first check-in?

title: An afternoon worth coming home to.
description:
A gardener and a mapmaker are both interested in what makes a place livable. Bram attends to what grows; Sera notices how people can move through it.

Bram knows a place by staying, and Sera by tracing its routes. Both welcome unhurried observation. Sera can ask planning questions without making Bram responsible for the decisions.

A question still to ask: would Bram enjoy Sera's occasional map talk, or prefer separate invitations? Their different interests are a reason to meet, not a promise that they will get along.

title: A plan, with room for an experiment
description: Mara and Leon are partners and Kit’s parents. They share stories and the work of parenting, while Mara prefers a clear timetable and Leon enjoys an optional detour. Both want separate invitations and individual placement decisions.

title: The map drawer and a patient pause
description: Mara is Kit’s documented guardian. They share maps and stories, although Kit’s lively curiosity and Mara’s measured pace need space alongside each other. The relationship does not substitute for Kit’s assent or a reviewed continuing-care plan.

title: An unfinished town is still a good afternoon
description: Leon and Kit enjoy stories and making cardboard places together. Leon is Kit’s parent and participates in the family care plan with Mara, the documented guardian. Shared play is optional, and Kit may stop or choose quiet without explaining.

title: A promising introduction is not permission to stay
description: No departed resident is placed alone: placements include at least two. Peer support reduces isolation; living relationships and an inhabited, maintained home anchor residents. Every resident and every relationship must meet the policy, with separate adult decisions, guardian care agreement and age-appropriate assent for dependent children. Hard boundaries come before preference scores; unknown required facts and unanswered introduction questions block a trial. No one owes work, care, performance, surveillance or a permanent stay.
